fields.Text: {{c1::Guided}} media: signals propagate in a solid medium (copper, fiber, coax). {{c2::Unguided}} media: signals propagate freely (e.g., radio).
Twisted pair: two insulated copper wires. Category 5 supports {{c1::100 Mbps and 1 Gbps}} Ethernet; Category 6 supports {{c2::10 Gbps}} Ethernet.
fields.Extra: The twisting reduces electrical interference from nearby pairs.

fields.Front: Describe coaxial cable and its key properties.
fields.Back: Two concentric copper conductors; bidirectional; broadband (multiple frequency channels on one cable), hundreds of Mbps per channel. Used by cable TV / cable Internet, can act as a shared medium.

fields.Front: What are the advantages of fiber optic cable?
fields.Back: Glass fiber carrying light pulses (each pulse a bit); high-speed point-to-point transmission (tens to hundreds of Gbps); low error rate: repeaters spaced far apart and immune to electromagnetic noise.

fields.Text: Fiber optic: each light pulse is a {{c1::bit}}; rates of {{c2::10s-100s of Gbps}}; immune to {{c3::electromagnetic noise}}.

fields.Front: What three propagation-environment effects affect wireless radio links?
fields.Back: Reflection, obstruction by objects, and interference.

fields.Front: Wireless radio links are described on the slides as 'broadcast' and what duplex mode?
fields.Back: Half-duplex (sender to receiver, one direction at a time); the signal is carried in the electromagnetic spectrum with no physical wire.

fields.Front: Give the rates for the four radio link types on the slides.
fields.Back: Terrestrial microwave: up to 45 Mbps per channel. Wireless LAN (WiFi): up to hundreds of Mbps. Wide-area cellular (4G): ~tens of Mbps. Satellite: up to 45 Mbps per channel, 270 ms end-to-end delay.

fields.Text: A geosynchronous satellite link has about {{c1::270 ms}} end-to-end delay; the two satellite types are {{c2::geosynchronous}} and {{c3::low-earth-orbit (LEO)}}.
fields.Extra: Geosynchronous satellites orbit ~36,000 km up; LEO satellites are much closer and have ~10 ms delays.
